## Company: International Container Terminal Services, Inc. (ICT)
Sector: Services / Transportation Services
International Container Terminal Services, Inc. (ICT) was incorporated on December 24, 1987 to operate, manage and develop the Manila International Container Terminal (MICT), which handles international container cargo at the Port of Manila. In May 1988, the Philippine Ports Authority awarded to ICT a concession to be the exclusive operator of MICT for a period of 25 years. ICT started operating MICT on June 12, 1988. ICT's concession contract for MICT was extended for another 25 years up to May 18, 2038.

The principal business of ICT is the operation, management, development, and acquisition of container terminals. The primary mechanism for the operation of these terminals is long-term concession agreements with local port authorities and governments through ICT and its subsidiaries. ICT and its subsidiaries also provide ancillary services such as storage, container stripping and stuffing, inspection, weighing and services for refrigerated containers or reefers, as well as roll-on/roll-off and anchorage services to non-containerized cargoes or general cargoes on a limited basis.

Currently, the ICT Group is involved in 32 terminal operations, including concessions and port development projects in 19 countries worldwide. There are 10 terminal operations in the Philippines- including an inland container terminal, a barge terminal, and combined terminal operations in Subic- four in Brazil; two in Papua New Guinea; and one each in China, Indonesia, Ecuador, Poland, Georgia, Madagascar, Croatia, Honduras, Mexico, Iraq, Argentina, Democratic Republic Congo, Colombia, Australia, Cameroon and Nigeria. 

Source: SEC Form 17-A (2024)

thesis:
International Container Terminal Services is one of the most understandable infrastructure businesses in the PSE universe. It operates container terminals — the chokepoints through which global trade physically moves — under long-term, exclusive concession agreements with governments and port authorities. With 32 terminal operations across 19 countries, and its flagship Manila International Container Terminal concession now extended to 2063, the business is simple, essential, and predictable: ships arrive, containers get processed, fees get collected. For a value investor, that predictability is the starting point.

The moat is as durable as moats get in the Philippines. Concession agreements are, by definition, government-sanctioned monopolies for their duration — a competitor cannot simply build a rival terminal at MICT and undercut ICTSI. The switching costs are structural: port infrastructure is immovable, and shipping lines build logistics networks around specific terminals. ICTSI's capital intensity and track record also function as a barrier; bidding against them for new concessions globally requires operational credibility that takes decades to build. The 29.9% 10-year average ROIC confirms the moat is real and not being eroded — returns above 15% sustained over a decade, in a capital-intensive infrastructure business, are exceptional.

Management quality here is high and verifiable. Enrique Razon Jr. has been building this business since 1987 and owns a controlling stake — the classic skin-in-the-game alignment. His 2026 posture is telling: while tariff uncertainty and global trade headwinds pushed many operators to trim capex, Razon committed to a $740M expansion plan and secured $300M in AIIB financing for further terminal development. H1 2026 results back the confidence: revenue up 27%, net income up 22%, TEU throughput up 15% year-on-year. The addition of Enrique Aboitiz as independent director adds a credible governance voice. One near-term management watch item is the rumored HK dual-listing — officially denied by both ICTSI and PSE leadership, but if it materializes it could affect local float and index weighting dynamics in ways worth monitoring.

Valuation is where the Rule #1 discipline bites. The current price of ₱982 sits slightly above the computed Sticker Price of ₱942 and 108% above the 50% Margin of Safety buy price of ₱471. The PEG of 0.67x suggests the market hasn't fully priced in the growth trajectory — impressive for a ₱2T market cap company — and the P/B of 0.3x is low for the quality on offer. But Rule #1's insistence on a 50% margin of safety exists precisely for situations like this: durable as the moat is, port concessions are exposed to sovereign risk, currency mismatches across 19 countries, and geopolitical disruptions (the Iraq and DRC terminals are not low-risk assets). The $300M AIIB debt and 2.09x D/E ratio are manageable given the cash-generative nature of concession businesses, but they leave limited room for macro stress. At current prices, you are paying for a great business at fair value, not a great business at a bargain.

Bottom line: ICTSI is a rare combination — globally diversified infrastructure moat, compounding management, and genuinely exceptional long-run returns. But at ₱982, fair value is what you get, not margin of safety. The Rule #1 investor watches this one and waits. A meaningful market correction, or a PSE-wide pullback that drags ICT toward the ₱700–800 range, would flip this to a strong buy. Until then, let the business keep compounding and revisit on weakness.
